Void
voyd
adj. and v.t. (empty, without content; also, annulled or of no effect; rendering Hebrew bohu, parar, Greek kenoo, katargeo)
From Old French voide, empty, from Latin vacuus. English keeps two senses that Scripture also keeps apart — empty of content, as in Genesis 1:2, and legally annulled, as in a vow or a covenant made void.

Biblical Definition

Void means empty, and Scripture uses it at the beginning, the middle, and the end of its argument. At the beginning: “the earth was without form, and void; and darkness was upon the face of the deep. And the Spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters” (Genesis 1:2) — the Hebrew pair tohu wa-bohu, unformed and unfilled, describing the raw material God then shapes and fills over six days, forming on days one to three and filling on days four to six. Jeremiah quotes the phrase back as a picture of judgment: “I beheld the earth, and, lo, it was without form, and void” (Jeremiah 4:23) — sin runs creation backwards. In the legal sense, a vow may be made void by a husband's word (Numbers 30:12), and men may make void the law of God, which draws the psalmist's cry: “It is time for thee, LORD, to work: for they have made void thy law” (Psalm 119:126). Paul uses the same category in his argument for grace: “if they which are of the law be heirs, faith is made void, and the promise made of none effect” (Romans 4:14) — law-keeping and promise cannot both be the ground, because each voids the other. And over against everything that can be voided stands God's word, which cannot: “it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please” (Isaiah 55:11).

Webster 1828 Definition

Empty, or annulled. The earth begins without form, and void and is formed and filled; sin runs that backwards in Jeremiah; men make void God's law; law-as-ground voids the promise; but God's word never returns void.

expand to see more

VOID, a. [Fr. vuide; L. viduus.] Empty; vacant; not occupied with any visible matter; as a void space or place.

2. Empty; unfurnished; unsupplied; wanting.

3. Having no legal or binding force; null; not effectual to bind parties; as a void contract.

4. Free; clear; as a conscience void of offence. Acts 24.

VOID, v.t. To make or leave vacant; to quit; to leave. 5. To annul; to nullify; to make of no validity or effect.

Key Scripture

Genesis 1:2 — "And the earth was without form, and void; and darkness was upon the face of the deep. And the Spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters."

Isaiah 55:11 — "So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it."

Psalm 119:126 — "It is time for thee, LORD, to work: for they have made void thy law."

Romans 4:14 — "For if they which are of the law be heirs, faith is made void, and the promise made of none effect:"

Modern Corruption

Genesis 1:2 is pressed into service for the gap theory — a ruined earlier creation between verses 1 and 2 — and Isaiah 55:11 is stretched into a general warrant that any words spoken in faith will accomplish what the speaker pleases.

expand to see more

The gap theory reads the earth was without form, and void as became void, inserting a fall of Satan and the destruction of a pre-Adamic world between the first two verses of the Bible. It was popularised by Chalmers and carried into wide currency by the Scofield notes, largely as a way of accommodating long geological ages. The Hebrew does not support it: the verb is the ordinary hayah with a waw-disjunctive, giving a circumstantial description of the earth as created rather than a subsequent catastrophe, and Exodus 20:11 states that in six days the LORD made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that in them is, leaving no room for a prior creation destroyed. The dictionary's position is the plain reading: tohu wa-bohu describes raw material at the outset of the week, unformed and unfilled, which God then forms on days one to three and fills on days four to six — a structure the chapter's own symmetry makes obvious.

Isaiah 55:11 has been annexed by the word-of-faith teaching, in which the principle that words do not return void is transferred from God to the believer, so that confession becomes creative and a spoken claim is expected to produce its object. Every term of the verse forbids it: my word, out of my mouth, that which I please, whereto I sent it. The efficacy belongs to the Sender, and the immediate context is the free pardon offered to the wicked who forsakes his way (v. 7). The comfort of the verse for a preacher or a parent is enormous and quite different from the promise being sold: the word of God that you scatter is not yours to make effectual, and it will not come back empty, though you may not live to see what it did.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew bohu (emptiness, void), paired with tohu (formlessness); parar (to break, annul, make void); Greek kenoo (to empty) and katargeo (to render inoperative).

expand to see more

Hebrew bohu (H922) — emptiness, void; occurring only three times, always with tohu (Genesis 1:2; Isaiah 34:11; Jeremiah 4:23).

Hebrew tohu (H8414) — formlessness, confusion, waste; used in Isaiah 45:18, where God says He created the earth not in vain (tohu).

Hebrew parar (H6565) — to break, frustrate, make void; the verb in Psalm 119:126 and in the annulling of vows in Numbers 30.

Greek kenoo (G2758) — to empty, make void; used in Romans 4:14 and, most weightily, of Christ emptying Himself in Philippians 2:7.

Greek katargeo (G2673) — to render idle or inoperative, make of none effect; the companion verb in Romans 4:14.

Usage

"“Without form, and void” — unformed and unfilled, the raw material God shapes and fills across the week."

"“They have made void thy law” — the psalmist's ground for asking God to act."

"“It shall not return unto me void” — the efficacy belongs to the Sender, not the speaker."
